title: Tata Motors Ltd. vs. Antonio Paulo Vaz & Anr. ((2021) 4 SCC 300)
text:
Tata Motors Ltd. vs. Antonio Paulo Vaz & Anr. ((2021) 4 SCC 300)
Court: Supreme Court of India
Facts: The consumer purchased a brand-new car manufactured by Tata Motors from an authorized dealership. Within days of delivery, the vehicle experienced severe mechanical breakdown and engine stalling. The dealer attempted repairs multiple times without success and refused to refund the purchase price or replace the vehicle.
Legal Issues: Whether a brand-new vehicle suffering from major breakdown within days constitutes a manufacturing defect under Consumer Protection Law?; Whether the product manufacturer can avoid vicarious product liability by citing principal-to-principal dealer contracts?
Consumer Supporting Principle: Inherent manufacturing defects in new goods entitle the consumer to full refund or replacement under Section 39.
Respondent Supporting Principle: Manufacturers are liable for replacement only when independent mechanical evidence proves an unrepairable manufacturing defect.
Court Reasoning: The Supreme Court held that delivering a brand-new vehicle with severe mechanical defects constitutes a fundamental breach of statutory consumer rights. Where a product suffers from an inherent manufacturing defect that cannot be rectified by routine repairs, forcing the consumer to accept a repaired car is unfair. The manufacturer and dealer are jointly liable.
Decision: Complaint Allowed in favour of the Consumer.
Relief: Ordered refund of the full purchase price of ₹8,50,000 along with 9% interest per annum from the date of purchase, plus ₹50,000 as compensation for mental agony and litigation costs.
tags: Tata Motors Ltd. vs. Antonio Paulo Vaz & Anr.

title: Amazon Seller Services Pvt. Ltd. vs. Vishwajit Singh (2022 NCDRC 412)
text:
Amazon Seller Services Pvt. Ltd. vs. Vishwajit Singh (2022 NCDRC 412)
Court: National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC)
Facts: The consumer ordered a high-end laptop on an online e-commerce marketplace platform during a sale. Upon opening the sealed package, the consumer received a brick instead of the laptop. Amazon refused to process a refund or replacement, claiming that the seller was a third-party entity and Amazon was merely an intermediary platform exempt from liability.
Legal Issues: Whether an e-commerce marketplace platform can claim intermediary immunity when a wrong/defective product is delivered?; Whether non-refund by an online platform constitutes an Unfair Trade Practice under Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020?
Consumer Supporting Principle: E-commerce platforms handling payments and fulfillment are accountable for non-delivery or wrong product delivery under Section 2(47) and E-Commerce Rules.
Respondent Supporting Principle: Pure intermediary platforms that do not manufacture or pack goods are exempt if prompt refund action is directed against the actual third-party seller.
Court Reasoning: The NCDRC ruled that under the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020, marketplace platforms that handle payment collection, logistics, and customer interface cannot disown responsibility for fraudulent non-delivery or defective shipments. Safe harbour under the IT Act does not override explicit duties under consumer protection law.
Decision: Revision Petition dismissed; Order against E-Commerce Platform Upheld.
Relief: Ordered immediate refund of ₹74,999 with 12% interest, plus ₹25,000 compensation and ₹10,000 litigation expenses.
tags: Amazon Seller Services Pvt. Ltd. vs. Vishwajit Singh

title: Horlicks Ltd. vs. Heinz India Pvt. Ltd. (2018 SCC OnLine Del 12975)
text:
Horlicks Ltd. vs. Heinz India Pvt. Ltd. (2018 SCC OnLine Del 12975)
Court: Delhi High Court
Facts: The defendant published comparative television and print advertisements claiming that one cup of Complan was equivalent to two cups of Horlicks in terms of growth protein, asserting '2x Faster Growth'. The claims were published without clinical validation standards acceptable under consumer advertising guidelines.
Legal Issues: Whether published commercial advertisements making unverified comparative performance claims constitute Misleading Advertisements under Consumer Law?; What evidentiary standards are required to prove a scientific growth claim made to public consumers?
Consumer Supporting Principle: Unsubstantiated scientific growth promises in mass advertisements violate consumer rights to accurate product information.
Respondent Supporting Principle: Truthful commercial puffery comparing nutritional values is permissible unless proven demonstrably false.
Court Reasoning: The Court held that commercial speech does not extend to making false or misleading representations regarding health or nutritional benefits. Advertisements that claim specific measurable outcomes (e.g. 2x growth) must be supported by proper scientific testing, failing which they constitute misleading advertisements under Section 2(28).
Decision: Injunction Granted against the Misleading Advertisement.
Relief: Restrained the opposite party from broadcasting or publishing the misleading growth comparison advertisement.

title: Indian Medical Association vs. V.P. Shantha & Ors. ((1995) 6 SCC 651)
text:
Indian Medical Association vs. V.P. Shantha & Ors. ((1995) 6 SCC 651)
Court: Supreme Court of India
Facts: A landmark medical negligence dispute where medical practitioners claimed that medical treatment provided by doctors does not fall within the scope of 'service' under consumer protection law, and patients cannot be treated as 'consumers'.
Legal Issues: Whether medical services rendered by medical practitioners and hospitals fall under 'service' under Section 2(42) of Consumer Protection Law?; Whether patients paying fees for medical treatment qualify as consumers entitled to claim compensation for medical deficiency?
Consumer Supporting Principle: Medical treatment rendered for financial consideration constitutes a statutory service under Section 2(42).
Respondent Supporting Principle: Free medical services rendered in government hospitals without consideration are excluded from consumer commission jurisdiction.
Court Reasoning: The Supreme Court delivered a historic judgment ruling that medical services rendered for remuneration fall squarely within the definition of 'service'. Patients paying for medical consultation or treatment are consumers, and medical negligence constitutes deficiency in service.
Decision: Landmark Ruling in favor of Consumer Protection Scope.
Relief: Affirmed the jurisdiction of Consumer Commissions to hear medical deficiency complaints and award compensation for medical negligence.

title: Lucknow Development Authority vs. M.K. Gupta ((1994) 1 SCC 243)
text:
Lucknow Development Authority vs. M.K. Gupta ((1994) 1 SCC 243)
Court: Supreme Court of India
Facts: A homebuyer deposited complete installments for a residential flat allotted by a public housing development authority. The authority failed to deliver possession of the flat for over 7 years beyond the agreed timeline and refused to pay interest or refund the money.
Legal Issues: Whether statutory development authorities providing housing plots/flats perform a 'service' under Consumer Law?; Whether inordinate delay in handing over possession of real estate constitutes Deficiency in Service entitling the homebuyer to refund with interest?
Consumer Supporting Principle: Delay in housing possession beyond the agreed timeline constitutes a statutory deficiency in service under Section 2(11).
Respondent Supporting Principle: Statutory authorities are exempt from penalty if delay occurred due to force majeure court injunctions outside the authority's control.
Court Reasoning: The Supreme Court held that housing construction and real estate development are express statutory services under consumer law. Public bodies cannot misbehave or cause unjust delay without accountability. Inordinate delay in possession is a classic deficiency in service.
Decision: Appeal Dismissed; Ruling in favor of Homebuyer.
Relief: Ordered immediate refund of deposited amount along with 18% interest per annum and punitive compensation against erring authority officials.
tags: Lucknow Development Authority vs. M.K. Gupta

title: State Bank of India vs. Ms. Sheila Ranganathan (2020 NCDRC 301)
text:
State Bank of India vs. Ms. Sheila Ranganathan (2020 NCDRC 301)
Court: National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC)
Facts: Unauthorised fraudulent ATM withdrawals took place from the consumer's bank account without OTP generation or SMS alerts sent to the mobile number. The bank refused to credit the fraudulently debited amount, claiming customer negligence in safeguarding PIN.
Legal Issues: Whether failure of a bank to send real-time SMS alerts and prevent unauthorized electronic transactions constitutes Deficiency in Service under Consumer Law?; Who bears the burden of proof for unauthorized banking transactions under RBI Circulars and Consumer Law?
Consumer Supporting Principle: Unauthorized electronic bank debits notified within 3 days carry zero liability for the consumer under Section 2(11).
Respondent Supporting Principle: Banks are not liable if documentary ATM log evidence proves PIN compromised directly by customer negligence.
Court Reasoning: The NCDRC held that banking institutions owe a strict duty of care to implement secure electronic payment systems. Where unauthorized transactions occur without SMS alert dispatch, the bank cannot penalize the account holder. Failure to credit zero-liability fraud within 10 days is a clear deficiency in service.
Decision: Order in favor of Account Holder.
Relief: Ordered State Bank of India to reverse the fraudulent debit of ₹1,20,000 with 9% interest and pay ₹20,000 compensation.

title: National Insurance Co. Ltd. vs. Harsolia Motors ((2023) 8 SCC 341)
text:
National Insurance Co. Ltd. vs. Harsolia Motors ((2023) 8 SCC 341)
Court: Supreme Court of India
Facts: A commercial entity took a fire insurance policy covering its business premises. Following a major fire damage, the insurance company repudiated the claim alleging that taking insurance for business assets is for 'commercial purpose' and therefore the firm is not a consumer under Section 2(7).
Legal Issues: Whether taking an insurance policy for indemnification against loss qualifies as a 'commercial purpose' excluding the policyholder from being a Consumer?; Whether arbitrary claim repudiation by an insurance company constitutes Deficiency in Service?
Consumer Supporting Principle: Insurance policyholders seeking indemnity for property damage qualify as consumers under Section 2(7).
Respondent Supporting Principle: Insurance repudiation is legally justified if surveyor reports establish material non-disclosure or policy condition breach.
Court Reasoning: The Supreme Court clarified that an insurance policy is taken for risk coverage and protection, not for trading or earning profit. Therefore, taking insurance for business premises does not convert the policy into a 'commercial purpose'. Arbitrary repudiation of valid claims is a deficiency in service.
Decision: Landmark Judgment in favor of Policyholders.
Relief: Set aside insurance repudiation; ordered full payment of assessed fire claim amount of ₹45,00,000 with 9% interest.

title: FIITJEE Ltd. vs. Minathi Rath (2012 NCDRC 188)
text:
FIITJEE Ltd. vs. Minathi Rath (2012 NCDRC 188)
Court: National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC)
Facts: A student enrolled in a 2-year coaching program and paid the full fee upfront. Due to unsatisfactory teaching standards, the student left the course within 3 months. The institute refused to refund the remaining 21 months' fee, citing a non-refundable clause in the enrollment agreement.
Legal Issues: Whether coaching institutes collecting advance non-refundable fees for multi-year courses commit an Unfair Trade Practice?; Whether non-refund of unavailed course fee when a student leaves midway constitutes Deficiency in Service?
Consumer Supporting Principle: Students leaving coaching courses midway are entitled to pro-rata refund of unearned fees under Section 2(47).
Respondent Supporting Principle: Institutes can retain reasonable registration fees and pro-rata tuition for the exact months attended by the student.
Court Reasoning: The NCDRC held that educational coaching institutions cannot collect advance fees for the entire duration of multi-year courses and retain unearned money. One-sided non-refundable clauses signed under compulsion are 'unfair contracts'. Institutes are entitled only to retain pro-rata fee for the period attended.
Decision: Revision Petition of Coaching Institute Dismissed.
Relief: Ordered coaching institute to refund the balance unearned fee of ₹1,15,000 along with 9% interest and ₹10,000 litigation costs.
